plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.7.5
plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates the change-of-variables transformation T for double integrals by showing a rectangular region in parameter space and its curved image in the xy-plane. Left panel: the uv-plane with a rectangular region S bounded by the lines u = u0, u = u0 + Delta_u (vertical) and v = v0, v = v0 + Delta_v (horizontal); the corner (u0, v0) and side lengths Delta_u and Delta_v are labeled. Right panel: the xy-plane with the image region R, a curved quadrilateral resembling a distorted parallelogram; each of the four boundary lines of S maps to a correspondingly labeled curve (Image of u = u0, Image of v = v0, etc.). A large arrow connects the two panels to indicate the transformation. The figure motivates the Jacobian as the factor relating the area of the rectangle S to the area of its curved image R under the transformation.

interactionPlan.concept: A change of variables T(u,v) = (x(u,v), y(u,v)) carries a small rectangle S in the uv-plane to a curved region R in the xy-plane, and the Jacobian determinant is the local factor by which the area is stretched.
elements: Left panel: uv-plane with black u-axis (horizontal, arrowhead right) and v-axis (vertical, arrowhead up), axis labels 'u' and 'v'
Left panel: two blue vertical grid lines labeled 'u = u₀' and 'u = u₀ + Δu', extending beyond the rectangle
Left panel: two blue horizontal grid lines labeled 'v = v₀' and 'v = v₀ + Δv', extending beyond the rectangle
Left panel: shaded light-blue rectangle S with blue outline, interior label 'S'
Left panel: four blue corner dots at the intersections of the grid lines
Left panel: corner label '(u₀, v₀)' at the lower-left corner
Left panel: side-length labels 'Δu' (below bottom edge) and 'Δv' (right of right edge)
Center: large curved pale-yellow/tan arrow with gray outline pointing from the left panel to the right panel, labeled 'T'
Right panel: xy-plane with black x-axis and y-axis, axis labels 'x' and 'y'
Right panel: curved quadrilateral region R, shaded light blue with thick blue boundary curves, interior label 'R'
Right panel: four boundary-curve labels with leaders — 'Image of u = u₀', 'Image of u = u₀ + Δu', 'Image of v = v₀', 'Image of v = v₀ + Δv'
Right panel: the four image curves extend slightly past the corners of R (as full coordinate curves)
Optional overlay: tangent vectors r_u Δu and r_v Δv at the image of (u₀, v₀) with the dashed parallelogram they span
Optional readout box: area(S) = ΔuΔv, |J(u₀,v₀)|, and approximate area(R) ≈ |J| Δu Δv

interactions.teaches: The shape of the image region is entirely determined by the mapping formulas; different formulas stretch, rotate, and bend the same rectangle in different ways.
interactions.label: Transformation T(u,v)

interactions.teaches: Moving or resizing S changes where and how much the map stretches area — the distortion is local, not global.
interactions.teaches_note: drag the lower-left corner to translate S, drag the upper-right corner to resize Δu and Δv

interactions.teaches: As Δu and Δv shrink, the curved image becomes indistinguishable from the parallelogram spanned by the tangent vectors — this is why the Jacobian appears in the integral.
interactions.label: Rectangle size (Δu = Δv)

interactions.teaches: The linear approximation of T at (u₀,v₀) replaces the curved region by a parallelogram whose area is |J|ΔuΔv.
interactions.label: Overlay

demo_steps.title: The rectangle S in the uv-plane
demo_steps.narration: On the left, the coordinate lines u = u₀, u = u₀ + Δu, v = v₀, v = v₀ + Δv cut out a plain rectangle S of area ΔuΔv. Nothing curved here — this is the easy domain we get to integrate over.

demo_steps.title: T bends the four edges
demo_steps.narration: The transformation x = u cos v, y = u sin v sends each straight edge of S to a coordinate curve: the u = const edges become circular arcs and the v = const edges become rays. The image R is a curved quadrilateral.

demo_steps.title: Move S — the distortion is local
demo_steps.narration: Drag S to a different corner of the uv-plane. The same formula stretches the rectangle by different amounts depending on where it sits, so the area factor must be a function of (u,v), not a constant.

demo_steps.title: Shrink S and the curves straighten
demo_steps.narration: Pull Δu and Δv toward zero. The image stops looking curved and becomes a tiny parallelogram — the local behavior of T is linear.

demo_steps.title: The Jacobian is the area factor
demo_steps.narration: Overlay the tangent vectors r_uΔu and r_vΔv at the image of (u₀,v₀). The parallelogram they span has area |∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)|ΔuΔv, which matches area(R) more and more exactly as the rectangle shrinks.

demo_steps.title: Try your own transformation
demo_steps.narration: Edit x(u,v) and y(u,v) — try x = u² − v², y = 2uv, or a shear x = u + v, y = v. Watch which maps preserve area (|J| = 1) and which blow it up or collapse it (|J| = 0).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A transformation is locally just a linear map, so an infinitesimal rectangle of area ΔuΔv becomes a parallelogram of area |∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)|ΔuΔv — the Jacobian is nothing more than that local area-stretching factor.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels on a white background, each with thin black axes (arrowheads at positive ends). Left panel labeled u (horizontal) and v (vertical); right panel labeled x and y. All curves, grid lines, region outlines and corner dots in a strong medium blue (~#1a9ad7); region interiors filled pale translucent blue (~#cfe7f5). Left panel shows a clean axis-aligned rectangle S sitting in the first quadrant, its four bounding blue lines extending noticeably past the rectangle corners, with black serif-italic math labels 'u = u₀', 'u = u₀ + Δu' above the vertical lines, 'v = v₀', 'v = v₀ + Δv' to the right of the horizontal lines, '(u₀, v₀)' at the lower-left corner, 'Δu' centered beneath the bottom edge and 'Δv' beside the right edge. Between the panels, a thick curved arrow arcing upward then right, filled pale cream/tan with a gray outline, optionally labeled T. Right panel shows R as a distorted quadrilateral with all four sides bowed — top and bottom edges curving one way, left and right edges the other — with the four image curves running past the corners; labels 'Image of u = u₀' (upper left), 'Image of u = u₀ + Δu' (top right), 'Image of v = v₀ + Δv' (right), 'Image of v = v₀' (lower right) with short leader lines to their curves, and a bold italic 'R' in the interior. In the tangent-parallelogram view, draw two arrows from the image of (u₀,v₀) in a contrasting color (orange/red) labeled r_uΔu and r_vΔv with a dashed parallelogram completing them, plus a small readout panel showing ΔuΔv, |J|, and |J|ΔuΔv vs. the true area of R. Equation input fields for x(u,v) and y(u,v) sit below the right panel with inline parse-error messages; corner drag handles on S appear as enlarged blue dots.

- equation input for the transformation: two fields for x(u,v) and y(u,v) pre-filled with a simple example (e.g. x=u*cos(v), y=u*sin(v)); learner edits either formula and the curved region R in the xy-plane redraws in real time while the rectangle S stays fixed — teaches that the Jacobian ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) measures how much the formula stretches area at each point
- drag the corners of rectangle S in the uv-plane and watch the image region R deform accordingly

authoredContext: To derive the change of variables formula for double integrals, we will need to understand the relationship between the area of a small rectangular region in the uv-plane and the area of its image in the xy-plane under a transformation T given by the equations x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v) For this purpose, suppose that _x000B_u and _x000B_v are positive, and consider a rectangular region S in the uv-plane enclosed by the lines u = u0,u = u0 + _x000B_u, v = v0,v = v0 + _x000B_v If the functions x(u, v) and y(u, v) are continuous, and if _x000B_u and _x000B_v are not too large, then the image of S in the xy-plane will be a region R that looks like a slightly distorted parallelogram (Figure 14.7.5). The sides of R are the constant u-curves and v-curves that correspond to the sides of S.

discrepancies: Right-panel curve labels are pushed to the far right edge of the canvas and connected by long thin leader lines; in the source each 'Image of ...' caption sits immediately beside the curve it names, so the generated version reads as a callout diagram rather than the original annotated figure.

The 'Image of u = u₀' caption sits on top of / immediately adjacent to the y-axis and the 'y' axis label, producing a collision that the source avoids (source places it clear of the axis with the curve reaching toward it).

All annotation text is rendered small inside a 1000×360 viewBox that is then shrunk to roughly half the page width, so the 14–16px labels ('u = u₀ + Δu', 'Image of v = v₀ + Δv', Δu/Δv) are uncomfortably small at inline size compared with the large, dominant labels in the source.

The generated R is a clean polar annular sector (circular arcs + straight radial rays) whereas the source R is a generically curved quadrilateral with all four sides bowed; the radial edges appear straight, weakening the 'all coordinate lines become curves' message at step 0.

Extra elements not in the source: a bold 'T' label on the transition arrow, thin grey leader lines, and (when toggled) an orange tangent-parallelogram/readout box — acceptable pedagogy but added chrome relative to the original.

In the left panel the blue coordinate lines extend only slightly past the rectangle, while the source shows them running conspicuously far beyond it (especially the vertical u-lines dropping below the region).
evaluation.notes: Composition, colors, and both panels closely track the source and the interaction set (demo steps, size slider, draggable corner handles, editable T(u,v) with presets, Jacobian overlay) is rich and pedagogically apt; the main weaknesses are undersized, leader-line-heavy right-panel captions with one collision against the y-axis, and a somewhat too-clean polar sector for R.
action_items: Place the four 'Image of ...' captions adjacent to the ends of their curves (as in the source) and drop the long leader lines, or shorten them drastically; nudge 'Image of u = u₀' away from the y-axis/'y' label to remove the collision.
Increase annotation font sizes (labels ≥18px in the 1000×360 viewBox) and/or narrow the UI panel so the SVG gets more width, so the Δu, Δv, and 'Image of ...' text is comfortably legible inline.
Extend the blue u = const and v = const coordinate lines further past the rectangle in the uv-plane to match the source's prominent crossing lines.

At step 0 use a default transformation whose image has all four boundary edges visibly curved (or add slight curvature to the radial edges) so R resembles the source's curved quadrilateral rather than a textbook polar sector.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual plan and interaction set are sound; all action items are concrete rendering fixes (label placement/size, leader lines, extended coordinate lines, curved boundary edges) that belong to the generator.

plan.concept: A change of variables T(u,v) = (x(u,v), y(u,v)) carries a small rectangle S in the uv-plane to a curved region R in the xy-plane, and the Jacobian determinant is the local factor by which the area is stretched.

interactions.teaches: The shape of the image region is entirely determined by the mapping formulas; different formulas stretch, rotate, and bend the same rectangle in different ways.
interactions.label: Transformation T(u,v)

interactions.teaches: Moving or resizing S changes where and how much the map stretches area — the distortion is local, not global.
interactions.teaches_note: drag the lower-left corner to translate S, drag the upper-right corner to resize Δu and Δv

interactions.teaches: As Δu and Δv shrink, the curved image becomes indistinguishable from the parallelogram spanned by the tangent vectors — this is why the Jacobian appears in the integral.
interactions.label: Rectangle size (Δu = Δv)

interactions.teaches: The linear approximation of T at (u₀,v₀) replaces the curved region by a parallelogram whose area is |J|ΔuΔv.
interactions.label: Overlay

demo_steps.title: The rectangle S in the uv-plane
demo_steps.narration: On the left, the coordinate lines u = u₀, u = u₀ + Δu, v = v₀, v = v₀ + Δv cut out a plain rectangle S of area ΔuΔv. Nothing curved here — this is the easy domain we get to integrate over.

demo_steps.title: T bends the four edges
demo_steps.narration: The transformation x = u cos v, y = u sin v sends each straight edge of S to a coordinate curve: the u = const edges become circular arcs and the v = const edges become rays. The image R is a curved quadrilateral.

demo_steps.title: Move S — the distortion is local
demo_steps.narration: Drag S to a different corner of the uv-plane. The same formula stretches the rectangle by different amounts depending on where it sits, so the area factor must be a function of (u,v), not a constant.

demo_steps.title: Shrink S and the curves straighten
demo_steps.narration: Pull Δu and Δv toward zero. The image stops looking curved and becomes a tiny parallelogram — the local behavior of T is linear.

demo_steps.title: The Jacobian is the area factor
demo_steps.narration: Overlay the tangent vectors r_uΔu and r_vΔv at the image of (u₀,v₀). The parallelogram they span has area |∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)|ΔuΔv, which matches area(R) more and more exactly as the rectangle shrinks.

demo_steps.title: Try your own transformation
demo_steps.narration: Edit x(u,v) and y(u,v) — try x = u² − v², y = 2uv, or a shear x = u + v, y = v. Watch which maps preserve area (|J| = 1) and which blow it up or collapse it (|J| = 0).

plan.keyInsight: A transformation is locally just a linear map, so an infinitesimal rectangle of area ΔuΔv becomes a parallelogram of area |∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)|ΔuΔv — the Jacobian is nothing more than that local area-stretching factor.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels on a white background, each with thin black axes (arrowheads at positive ends). Left panel labeled u (horizontal) and v (vertical); right panel labeled x and y. All curves, grid lines, region outlines and corner dots in a strong medium blue (~#1a9ad7); region interiors filled pale translucent blue (~#cfe7f5). Left panel shows a clean axis-aligned rectangle S sitting in the first quadrant, its four bounding blue lines extending noticeably past the rectangle corners, with black serif-italic math labels 'u = u₀', 'u = u₀ + Δu' above the vertical lines, 'v = v₀', 'v = v₀ + Δv' to the right of the horizontal lines, '(u₀, v₀)' at the lower-left corner, 'Δu' centered beneath the bottom edge and 'Δv' beside the right edge. Between the panels, a thick curved arrow arcing upward then right, filled pale cream/tan with a gray outline, optionally labeled T. Right panel shows R as a distorted quadrilateral with all four sides bowed — top and bottom edges curving one way, left and right edges the other — with the four image curves running past the corners; labels 'Image of u = u₀' (upper left), 'Image of u = u₀ + Δu' (top right), 'Image of v = v₀ + Δv' (right), 'Image of v = v₀' (lower right) with short leader lines to their curves, and a bold italic 'R' in the interior. In the tangent-parallelogram view, draw two arrows from the image of (u₀,v₀) in a contrasting color (orange/red) labeled r_uΔu and r_vΔv with a dashed parallelogram completing them, plus a small readout panel showing ΔuΔv, |J|, and |J|ΔuΔv vs. the true area of R. Equation input fields for x(u,v) and y(u,v) sit below the right panel with inline parse-error messages; corner drag handles on S appear as enlarged blue dots.

discrepancies: Right panel: the caption 'Image of u = u₀' is anchored at a fixed x and collides with the y-axis and the italic 'y' axis label (visible overlap in the screenshot), whereas in the source it sits clearly to the left of the curve with no overlap.

The curved transition arrow is placed too far left: its tail overlaps the left panel's u-axis arrowhead and crowds the 'v = v₀' / 'Δu' labels, while in the source the arrow occupies clear white space between the two panels.

Region R is drawn noticeably smaller relative to its panel than in the source, and the blue coordinate curves extend only slightly past the corners, so the characteristic 'four long crossing curves' look of the source is weaker.

Overall glyph sizes are small at inline display (the 1120-unit viewBox is squeezed into roughly half the page width next to a wide control panel), making the 'Image of …' captions and the u/v axis letters harder to read than the large serif labels in the source.

The left panel's blue coordinate lines are shorter than in the source, so the crossing lines read less like an infinite grid family; corner dots are present but the extension beyond the rectangle is minimal.
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful two-panel change-of-variables figure with correct colors, curves and a rich, genuinely pedagogical interaction set (drag handles, size slider, Jacobian overlay, editable T, 6-step tour), but label placement is sloppy — 'Image of u = u₀' collides with the y-axis label and the transition arrow crowds the left panel's u-axis — and text is small at inline size.
action_items: Reposition the 'Image of u = u₀' caption (and add collision avoidance against the drawn axes/axis letters) so no caption overlaps the y-axis line or the 'y' label; consider computing caption anchors from the curve endpoints rather than hard-coded x/y.
Shift the transition arrow right (start it past the left panel's u-axis arrowhead) or shorten the left u-axis so the arrow tail no longer overlaps axis geometry and the 'v = v₀' / 'Δu' labels.

Increase label font sizes (or reduce the viewBox width / narrow the UI panel) so the 'Image of …' captions and axis letters remain comfortably legible at inline display width, and keep the S/R interior labels visibly larger than the captions as in the source.
Extend the blue coordinate lines/curves further beyond the rectangle and the region on both panels, and enlarge R's fit box, to better match the source's proportions.
